MEDI2200 · Week 8 · Mutations and repair

Mutations & DNA Repair how the code breaks & how the cell mends it

This guide closes the "building cell components" arc by asking what happens when DNA goes wrong — from a single swapped base to a whole missing chromosome — and how the cell's repair crews put it right before the damage becomes a lasting mutation.

Covers Parts 1–3 of the module Figures 15 plates from the iLearn book Self-tests interactive

How to use this guide

Every subsection has a reference code like §4.3 — quote it to go deeper on exactly that piece. Each figure from the module appears as a numbered Plate with a Label Key decoding what's in it. The coloured tags carry the extras:

Reasoning

§0Part 1 · Introduction

Mutation versus repair

Two opposing forces decide whether a chemical accident in your DNA becomes a permanent change.

We have spent the term building cell components — nucleic acids, then the proteins they encode. This week flips the lens: we look at how those instructions go wrong (a mutation) and at the machinery that fixes them (repair). The centre of gravity is genetic mutations — changes to DNA — and the downstream consequence for the proteins that are produced. Get that cause-and-effect chain and the whole module falls into place.

The two learning objectives are deliberately paired: (1) describe the types of DNA mutation and their effects on protein function, and (2) describe the major DNA repair pathways. Read the guide as one argument — a mutation is only a problem if repair fails to catch it first, so the damage in §4 is the cause and the mutations in §2–§3 are what happens when the repair crews miss it.

Reasoning · why study mutation and repair together

Damage to DNA is constant — every cell takes tens of thousands of chemical hits a day. The reason your genome is stable anyway is that damage and repair are a matched pair: a lesion is a transient chemical change, but it only becomes a heritable mutation if it is copied by replication before it is repaired. Studying them apart hides the single most important idea of the week — timing. Repair races replication.

Clinical / real-world

This is not abstract. Lose a repair pathway and mutations accumulate — the same logic underlies cancers of repair-deficiency you will meet later (Lynch syndrome from broken mismatch repair, xeroderma pigmentosum from broken UV repair, BRCA cancers from broken break-repair). The module even ends with a lecture quiz on exactly this material. The presenters are Dr Lucinda McRobb and Dr Christine Chiu.

§1Part 2 · Genetic variation

What is a mutation?

A permanent change to DNA — but whether your children inherit it depends on which cell it happens in.

A mutation is a permanent change in the amount or structure of genetic material (DNA). That one definition already contains the whole taxonomy to come: a change in amount foreshadows insertions, deletions and whole-chromosome gains (§2, §3); a change in structure foreshadows substitutions and rearrangements. Mutations happen three ways — during DNA replication, via homologous recombination during meiosis, or from environmental exposure (chemicals, radiation).

Mutations can be inherited or arise spontaneously, and they split into two families defined entirely by which cell they occur in. Plate 1.1 draws the distinction the way you should hold it in memory — a body cell on one side, a gamete on the other.

Label Key — where the mutation lands decides everything
Somatic cells
Any body cell that is not an egg or sperm — the neuron shown is the example. A mutation here cannot be passed to offspring; it affects only that cell and its descendants in the same body. Matters because most cells you have are somatic, so most mutations you accumulate stay with you.
Germline (germinal) cells
The egg and sperm — cells that develop into ovum or sperm. A mutation here can be inherited by offspring. Matters because these are the only mutations that enter the family tree and drive genetic disease across generations.
🤔 Predict · before you read on

If genetic variation between people — and even between cells in one person — is extremely common, why aren't we all riddled with disease?

Because the vast majority of mutations are harmless. Most fall in non-coding DNA or are silent, so they have no effect on the gene's function or the overall phenotype. Variation is the background state of the genome, not the exception — disease comes from the rare mutation that lands in the wrong place.
Reasoning · why the somatic/germline line is drawn at the gamete

Inheritance is physical: a trait can only reach a child through the one egg or sperm that forms them. A mutation in a skin cell never enters that gamete, so it is a dead end for heredity (though not for that person — see below). The germline is the genome's bottleneck to the future, which is exactly why the cell guards it so heavily.

Clinical / real-world

Both matter, but differently. A somatic mutation can't be inherited yet can still cause disease in you — most cancers begin as somatic mutations in a single body cell. A germline mutation is what a genetic counsellor traces through a pedigree, because it is present in every cell (including the gametes) and can recur in each generation.

§2Part 2 · Genetic variation

Single-gene mutations

The smallest changes — one base at a time — and how they ripple out to the protein.

We start small — literally at single base pairs — because these are the atoms of the whole subject. Every larger event in §3 is built from the same moves: adding DNA, losing DNA, or swapping it. Get the three raw operations first, then trace them forward into what they do to the protein.

§2.1Substitution, deletion, insertion

Three raw operations describe every single-gene change, and Plate 2.1 shows all three against a reference allele so you can see what "same length" versus "gain" versus "loss" looks like on the sequence.

Label Key — reading Plate 2.1
Substitution (top)
One nucleotide replaced by another, with no net gain or loss of DNA — the highlighted base differs but the length is unchanged. This is the most common single-gene change and the workhorse of point mutations below.
Insertion (middle)
A gain of DNA — the highlighted base is extra. Small duplications are a type of insertion. Matters because it lengthens the sequence and, if not a multiple of three, wrecks the reading frame.
Deletion (bottom)
A loss of DNA (the blank squares) — from a single base up to many thousands. Matters for the same frame reason and because losing coding DNA can delete function outright.
  • Substitution — replacement of a single nucleotide by another with no net gain or loss of DNA. Arises from mistakes during DNA replication, during DNA repair, or most commonly from spontaneous deamination of methylated cytosine to thymine (a chemistry you will meet again as a form of damage in §4.1).
  • Deletion — loss of DNA, from one to many thousands of nucleotides. Sequences near chromosome ends (telomeres) are often similar to one another, which predisposes them to recombination errors that delete the DNA between them.
  • Insertion — a gain of DNA. Small duplications (a type of insertion) occur when repeated sequences are mistakenly duplicated during replication via replication slippage — the polymerase stutters over a repeat and copies it twice.
Reasoning · why deletions and insertions cluster at repeats

Both the telomere-recombination and the replication-slippage stories share one cause: repeated, similar sequences. When two stretches of DNA look alike, the machinery can mis-align them — pairing repeat #1 with repeat #3 instead of its true partner. The mis-alignment then either loops out a chunk (deletion) or copies one twice (insertion/duplication). So repetitive DNA is the structural weak point where "amount" mutations are born.

§2.2Structural effects on the protein

A change in the DNA only matters if it changes the protein, and that depends on how the altered codon reads. Plate 2.2 lines up DNA, mRNA and the resulting protein for each outcome — trace one row at a time to see why some swaps are invisible and others catastrophic.

Label Key — the four fates in Plate 2.2
Reference (top row)
The unmutated DNA/mRNA/protein — Met Ala Gly Lys Cys Arg Gly Val. Every other row is read against this.
Silent
The base changes but the codon still specifies the same amino acid — the protein is identical. Matters because it shows the genetic code's redundancy protects against many swaps.
Missense
The codon now specifies a different amino acid, which is built into the chain. One residue changes — sometimes harmless, sometimes disease-defining.
Frameshift
An indel that is not a multiple of three shifts the reading frame, so every downstream codon and amino acid changes — here the whole tail becomes gibberish (Gln Val Ser Trp Cys).
Nonsense
A codon becomes a stop codon (the ∗) — translation ends early. The truncated mRNA is usually degraded and no protein is made.
  • Silent — a point mutation with no effect on the amino-acid sequence.
  • Missense — the codon codes for a different amino acid, which is incorporated into the peptide chain.
  • Frameshift — insertions and deletions, if not a multiple of three, shift the reading frame so the whole downstream amino-acid sequence is altered.
  • Nonsense — a codon is converted to a stop codon (UAG, UAA, UGA). The nonsense mRNA is typically truncated, mostly subjected to degradation, and no protein product is formed.
Reasoning · why "multiple of three" is the make-or-break rule

The ribosome reads mRNA in non-overlapping triplets from a fixed start. Add or remove a number of bases divisible by three and the frame survives — you simply gain or lose whole codons. Add or remove any other number and every triplet boundary downstream shifts by one or two, so from the mutation onward the ribosome reads an entirely different set of codons. That is why a single-base insertion is usually far more destructive than a three-base one: it isn't the size, it's the divisibility.

Memory hook · the four S/M/F/N fates

"Silent says nothing, Missense says the wrong word, Nonsense stops the sentence, Frameshift scrambles the rest."

Rank of typical severity for a coding change: silent < missense < frameshift ≈ nonsense — because the last two usually destroy everything downstream.

Clinical / real-world · sickle-cell disease

The archetypal missense mutation is sickle-cell disease: a single A→T substitution in the β-globin gene swaps glutamate for valine at position 6. One changed residue — exactly the missense row of Plate 2.2 — makes haemoglobin polymerise when deoxygenated, deforming red cells into sickles. It proves the guide's whole thesis: a permanent change in DNA structure, one base wide, propagates all the way to protein function and a clinical phenotype.

§2.3Triplet repeat expansions & splice-site mutations

Two special single-gene mechanisms don't fit the tidy point-mutation picture. The first is a runaway of the repeat problem from §2.1.

Triplet (trinucleotide) repeat expansions typically involve cytosine/guanine-rich triplets — CGG, CCG, CAG, CTG — that can run from a few copies to several thousand. Repeats over 28 are unstable during replication, and the instability increases with the number of repeats already present. New expansions are produced during replication, so the repeat count changes across successive generations. That is the mechanism behind anticipation: the disorder appears at an earlier age with each generation. Huntington's disease is the example — the higher the CAG repeat number, the earlier the onset and the more severe the symptoms, as Plate 2.3 quantifies.

Label Key — reading Plate 2.3
x-axis (repeat length)
Number of CAG triplets, ~30 to ~100. Moving right = a longer, more unstable expansion.
y-axis (age at onset)
Age in years when symptoms appear. The steep downward cloud shows onset falling as repeats rise — the graphical face of anticipation.
The trend line
Summarises the inverse relationship: more repeats → earlier onset. Because expansions grow each generation, children inherit longer runs and fall further left-and-down than their parents.

The second special case sits at the boundaries between exons. Recall that nucleotide sequences at the splice site (intron–exon boundaries) guide the spliceosome to where exons will be joined. Mutations within these sequences can cause the mature mRNA to retain introns, or lose exons. Plate 2.4 contrasts normal splicing (panel A) with a splice-site mutation (panel B) that skips an exon.

Label Key — Plate 2.4
Exons / introns
Coding blocks (exons 1–3) separated by introns 1–2. Splicing must remove introns and join exons in order.
GT…AG splice signals
The conserved intron-boundary sequences that the spliceosome recognises. These are the letters a splice-site mutation corrupts.
Panel A — normal splicing
Introns are excised at the correct GT…AG sites (arrows) and the three exons join cleanly — the reference outcome.
Panel B — mutant
The changed boundary sequence mis-guides the spliceosome, so the transcript is spliced wrongly — an exon is lost (or an intron retained). Matters because a single boundary base can delete a whole coding block from the protein.
Reasoning · why expansions get worse each generation

The instability is self-amplifying. A long run of identical triplets is exactly the repetitive template that lets replication slip (§2.1) — and the longer the run, the more chances to slip, so long alleles expand faster than short ones. Because the expanded allele is what gets passed on, each generation starts from a longer, even more slippage-prone run. Cause (repeats) feeds mechanism (slippage) feeds consequence (earlier onset) in a loop — the definition of anticipation.

Clinical / real-world · Huntington's & the CAG threshold

Huntington's disease is autosomal dominant: CAG expansions in the HTT gene above the ~36–40 threshold cause a toxic polyglutamine protein. Plate 2.3's slope is why a mildly affected parent with ~40 repeats can have a child with juvenile-onset disease at ~60 repeats — the expansion grew in transmission. Splice-site mutations are equally clinical: many β-thalassaemia and cystic-fibrosis alleles are splice-site changes that quietly delete an exon.

§2.4Functional effects of mutations

Step back from how the sequence changed to what it does to the amount and behaviour of protein. Plate 2.5 sorts every mutation into three functional buckets by comparing the mutant allele's product with the normal allele's.

Label Key — the three functional classes in Plate 2.5
Gain-of-function (top)
The mutant allele (starred) produces a novel or excess protein product — note the extra protein clusters. Matters because it can be dominant: one over-active allele is enough.
Loss-of-function (middle)
The mutant allele's arrow leads to no product — protein output is reduced or eliminated. Often recessive, because the normal allele may still supply enough.
Dominant-negative (bottom)
The mutant allele makes an abnormal product that interferes with the normal protein made by allele 1 (the two tangle together). Matters because a bad subunit can poison a whole complex, so even a heterozygote is affected.
Functional classes — what the mutant allele does to protein
ClassEffect on productTypical inheritance logic
Gain-of-functionNovel or excess proteinOften dominant — one over-active allele suffices
Loss-of-functionReduced or eliminated proteinOften recessive — the normal allele can compensate
Dominant-negativeAbnormal protein that interferes with the normal oneDominant — the bad product sabotages the good
Reasoning · why a dominant-negative beats a simple loss

A loss-of-function heterozygote still has one working allele, so half-normal protein is often enough — the phenotype is mild or absent. A dominant-negative is worse because the mutant product doesn't just do nothing; it actively binds and disables the normal product. In a protein that works as a multi-subunit complex, incorporating even one faulty subunit can inactivate the whole assembly — so the defect spreads from the bad allele to the good one. Same 50% mutant DNA, far worse outcome.

Clinical / real-world · loss-of-function & cystic fibrosis

Cystic fibrosis is the classic loss-of-function, recessive disease: mutations in CFTR (most often ΔF508, a three-base deletion) yield little or no working chloride channel, so two defective alleles are needed to cause disease. Contrast osteogenesis imperfecta, where a single dominant-negative collagen allele produces a faulty chain that ruins the whole triple helix — showing exactly why the bottom panel of Plate 2.5 is the most damaging class.

R Recall — single-gene mutations
  • Substitution — swaps a base with no net gain or loss of DNA; most often from deamination of methylated cytosine to thymine.
  • Frameshift rule — an indel changes the reading frame only when it is not a multiple of three.
  • Nonsense — makes a premature stop codon; mRNA is truncated and degraded, so no protein.
  • Anticipation — triplet expansions grow each generation, so onset comes earlier; the example is Huntington's (CAG).
  • Dominant-negative — the mutant product interferes with the normal protein, unlike a simple loss-of-function.
§3Part 2 · Genetic variation

Chromosome mutations

Zoom out from single bases to whole chromosomes — mistakes in number and in structure.

Having built up from single bases, we now scale up to the largest genetic changes: whole chromosomes. A complete human karyotype is 46 chromosomes — 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes. Karyotypes with an abnormal number of chromosomes can have serious and sometimes lethal consequences. Two questions organise the section: is the number wrong (§3.1), or is the structure wrong (§3.2)?

§3.1Variation in number — aneuploidy

Aneuploidy is an abnormal chromosome number, and its most common cause is nondisjunction — the failure of chromosomes to segregate properly during meiosis. It can happen at anaphase I or II and produces gametes with missing or additional chromosomes. Fertilise such a gamete with a normal one and you get a trisomy (an extra copy) or a monosomy (a missing copy), as Plate 3.1 traces from parent to offspring.

Label Key — following the failure in Plate 3.1
Meiosis I nondisjunction (left)
The homologous pair fails to separate in the first division, so both go to one cell. Result: two gametes get both, two get neither.
Meiosis II nondisjunction (right)
Sister chromatids fail to separate in the second division — only some gametes are affected. Matters because the stage of failure sets how many gametes end up abnormal.
Fertilisation with a normal gamete
A normal (single-copy) gamete joins each abnormal one, converting a gamete imbalance into an offspring karyotype.
Trisomy
Offspring with an extra chromosome (three copies) — from a gamete that carried two.
Monosomy
Offspring with a missing chromosome (one copy) — from a gamete that carried none.
Reasoning · why nondisjunction gives paired opposite outcomes

Meiosis is a partitioning of a fixed set of chromosomes. If a pair fails to separate, the chromosomes don't vanish — they simply go to the wrong side. So every nondisjunction event necessarily makes a matched pair of errors: a gamete with too many and a gamete with too few. That symmetry is why trisomy and monosomy always appear together in Plate 3.1, one on each branch — it is conservation of chromosomes playing out.

Clinical / real-world · Down syndrome & the viability gap

Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) is the best-known aneuploidy, caused by nondisjunction of chromosome 21 — usually in meiosis I of the egg, which is why risk rises with maternal age. Notice the asymmetry Plate 3.1 hints at: most monosomies are lethal early (too little gene dosage to survive), whereas some trisomies of gene-poor chromosomes (13, 18, 21) can reach term. Turner syndrome (45,X) is the one viable human monosomy.

§3.2Variation in structure — translocations

The other way to break a chromosome is to change its structure. Structural abnormalities are rearrangements of genetic material that alter the structure of the chromosome, and they come in two flavours: balanced (no gain or loss of chromosomal material) or unbalanced (a gain or loss of material). Plate 3.2 shows two translocation types.

Label Key — Plate 3.2
Balanced reciprocal (top)
Two chromosomes swap segments at the break points (arrowheads); all the material is still present, just rearranged — hence balanced.
Robertsonian / centric fusion (bottom)
Two chromosomes fuse at the centromere into one; the small fragments are lost. Matters because this changes chromosome number and can be passed on with reproductive consequences.

Structure only becomes a fertility problem at meiosis. In a carrier of a balanced translocation, pairing of homologous regions in meiosis I forms a quadrivalent — the bent, cross-like structure in Plate 3.3. The quadrivalent shape lets the two derivative chromosomes align with their homologues so that homologous recombination (prophase I) can occur before segregation. How the quadrivalent then splits decides the gametes.

Label Key — Plate 3.3 (panels A, B, C)
A — Chromosomes
The normal pair (A, B) plus their derivatives der(A), der(B) made by the translocation. These four must all find partners at meiosis.
B — Quadrivalent formation
Because no single chromosome is fully homologous to another, all four line up in a cross so every region pairs with its match — the only geometry that lets them synapse.
C — Segregation & gametes
Three ways the cross can split: Adjacent-1 and Adjacent-2 each give only unbalanced gametes; only Alternate segregation yields a normal and a balanced gamete. Matters because only these balanced gametes make a normal-phenotype child.

Reading Plate 3.3C left to right: Adjacent-1 segregation leads only to unbalanced gametes; Adjacent-2 segregation leads only to unbalanced gametes; only Alternate segregation can lead to balanced gametes. Because only alternate-segregation gametes produce offspring with a normal phenotype, individuals carrying translocations have reduced fertility.

Reasoning · why a "balanced" carrier is healthy but subfertile

Here is the twist students miss: a balanced-translocation carrier is usually healthy — they have all their genes, just rearranged, so their own cells work fine. The problem only shows up in the next generation. Meiosis has to divide the quadrivalent, and two of the three ways of splitting it (adjacent-1 and adjacent-2) hand the gamete a der chromosome without its partner — an unbalanced set. Those embryos are lost or affected. So the carrier's fertility falls not because they are ill, but because most of their gametes are chromosomally unbalanced.

Clinical / real-world · recurrent miscarriage & translocation Down syndrome

Balanced-translocation carriers typically present not with their own illness but with recurrent miscarriage or infertility — the unbalanced gametes of Plate 3.3 fail to implant or miscarry. A Robertsonian translocation involving chromosome 21 can also produce translocation Down syndrome that recurs in families independently of maternal age, distinguishing it from the nondisjunction trisomy 21 of §3.1.

R Recall — chromosome mutations
  • Karyotype — 46 chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes + 1 pair of sex chromosomes.
  • Aneuploidy — an abnormal chromosome number, most commonly caused by nondisjunction in meiosis.
  • Nondisjunction outcomes — trisomy (extra) and monosomy (missing) after fertilisation with a normal gamete.
  • Balanced vs unbalanced — balanced has no net gain or loss; unbalanced has a gain or loss of material.
  • Translocation fertility — only alternate segregation gives balanced gametes, so carriers have reduced fertility.
§4Part 3 · DNA damage and repair

DNA damage & repair

Damage is the cause; the four repair pathways are the defence that stops it becoming a mutation.

Now the payoff. Every mutation in §2–§3 begins as damage — and whether that damage becomes a permanent mutation depends entirely on whether repair catches it first. We build this section as the cause–mechanism–consequence chain promised in §0: what damages DNA (§4.1), the shared logic of repair (§4.2), then the four specific pathways, each tuned to a different kind of lesion (§4.3–§4.6).

§4.1Types of DNA damage

Mutations can result from incorporating incorrect bases during replication, or from chemicals or radiation that change the DNA's chemical structure. Common examples: depurination, deamination, and thymine dimers; the addition of methyl or ethyl groups to bases (alkylation); or the formation of adducts, when chemical groups bind DNA. All of these disrupt normal base pairing and DNA replication.

The crucial idea — the hinge of the whole week — is that damage only becomes a mutation if it is left unrepaired and then copied. Plate 4.1 shows two lesions playing out through replication.

Label Key — Plate 4.1
Depurinated A (left)
A purine is lost, leaving a gap. On replication the machinery may skip the missing base (an A–T pair is deleted) or place a wrong base opposite it (a substitution). Shows one lesion, two possible mutations.
Deaminated C (right)
Cytosine loses its amino group and reads like a different base, so on replication a G has been changed to an A — a substitution. This is the same deamination chemistry named as the top cause of substitutions in §2.1.
"mutated" vs "unchanged" strands
Only the strand copied from the damaged template inherits the error; the other daughter is normal — proof that the mutation is fixed in by replication, not by the damage itself.
Reasoning · why timing (repair vs replication) decides the outcome

A depurinated site or a deaminated base is, for the moment, just a chemical blemish — reversible if a repair enzyme reaches it first. The moment becomes permanent only when a polymerase reads the damaged template and lays down a wrong (or absent) partner in the new strand. After that, the "wrong" base is now a legitimate, base-paired part of the sequence and looks correct to every future check. So repair has a deadline — the next round of replication — and everything in §4.2 onward is about meeting it.

Clinical / real-world · why UV and smoke are mutagens

The damage list is a mutagen list. UV light forms thymine (pyrimidine) dimers; tobacco smoke and many chemicals form bulky adducts; both distort the helix and, unrepaired, become the substitutions and deletions of Plate 4.1. This is why the repair pathways below are literally cancer-prevention machinery — and why losing one (as in §4.5's xeroderma pigmentosum) turns everyday sunlight into a carcinogen.

§4.2The common logic of repair

DNA is the repository of genetic information in every cell, so its integrity is essential; replication errors and environmental damage must be repaired to avoid mutation and disease. Eukaryotic cells have several detection-and-repair mechanisms, but they all share the same three steps:

  1. Excise — the segment of the damaged strand is cut out.
  2. Fill — a repair DNA polymerase fills in the missing nucleotides on the damaged strand, using the intact complementary strand as a template.
  3. Seal — DNA ligase seals the remaining nick, restoring the backbone.
Reasoning · why the intact strand is the secret to accurate repair

Double-stranded DNA is redundant by design: each strand specifies the other. That redundancy is what makes excision repair trustworthy — cut out the damaged stretch and the correct sequence is still readable on the partner strand, so the polymerase can rebuild the exact original. This single principle explains why the base-, nucleotide- and mismatch-repair pathways are all accurate, and why a double-strand break (§4.6) — where both templates are gone at once — is so much more dangerous and harder to fix.

§4.3Mismatch repair (MMR)

Mismatch repair is the cell's backup proof-reader. DNA polymerase proof-reads as it copies, but it is not perfect — occasionally a wrong base slips through, e.g. an A paired with a C. MMR catches these. Crucially it is strand-specific: it only targets the newly made (daughter) strand, because the original strand carries the correct sequence. Specialised proteins recognise the error, bind the daughter strand, then loop out and scan the DNA until they find a nearby GATC sequence / nick, where the strand is cut. Exonucleases then digest the daughter strand from that cut all the way past the mismatch; single-stranded binding proteins stabilise the exposed region; DNA polymerase fills in the correct bases and ligase seals. Plate 4.2 follows the MutS/MutL proteins through this.

Label Key — Plate 4.2
Error in the newly made strand
The mismatch (wrong base) in the daughter strand — the target of the whole pathway.
MutS / MutL
The mismatch-proofreading proteins: MutS recognises and binds the mismatch, MutL joins to coordinate the scan. Human versions of these are the genes lost in Lynch syndrome (below).
Scanning to the nick
The proteins track along until they hit a nick in the new strand — the signal marking which strand to cut.
Strand removal
Exonucleases digest the daughter strand from the nick past the mismatch, deleting the error.
Repair synthesis
Polymerase re-copies the stretch from the intact template and ligase seals it — the general 3-step logic of §4.2 applied.

How does the machinery know which strand to cut? In eukaryotes the clue is transient nicks in the new strand — from Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand, and from the leading strand where it joins the lagging strand at the next replication fork. These nicks flag the strand to fix. One limitation is efficiency: if the nearest GATC/nick is far away, hundreds or thousands of bases may be removed and re-synthesised just to correct a single wrong base.

Reasoning · why "which strand" is the whole problem

At a mismatch, one base is right and one is wrong — but chemically they look identical, both properly bonded. If MMR guessed wrong and "corrected" the original strand, it would convert the error into a permanent mutation instead of fixing it. So the entire pathway hinges on strand discrimination: the nicks in the freshly made strand are the only trustworthy label for "this is the new, error-prone copy." Take away the label and repair becomes as likely to break DNA as to mend it.

Clinical / real-world · Lynch syndrome (HNPCC)

Lose MMR and mutation rates skyrocket. Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC / Lynch syndrome) is caused by mutations in the human versions of the bacterial MutS and MutL proteins; affected individuals have mutation rates over 100 times higher than normal, driving early colorectal (and other) cancers. It is the cleanest illustration of the module's thesis — a broken repair pathway is itself a cause of cancer.

§4.4Base excision repair (BER)

BER is precision repair for small, subtle damage to a single base — the products of oxidation, deamination or alkylation. Think of fixing one faulty brick rather than rebuilding the wall. It runs, as Plate 4.3 shows, through a specific relay of enzymes.

Label Key — Plate 4.3
Deaminated C → U
The lesion: a cytosine deaminated to uracil, which no longer belongs in DNA.
Uracil DNA glycosylase
A DNA glycosylase — each type recognises one kind of damaged base. It snips the bond between the faulty base and the sugar, leaving an abasic (AP) site (sugar present, base gone).
AP endonuclease + phosphodiesterase
AP endonuclease cuts the strand at the abasic site; the phosphodiesterase removes the leftover sugar-phosphate, leaving a clean single-nucleotide gap.
DNA polymerase + ligase
Polymerase inserts the correct nucleotide using the intact strand as template; ligase seals the nick — backbone restored.

So BER is a highly targeted process: detect the wrong base, cut it out, clean the site, and rebuild it with the right nucleotide. Without BER, even tiny chemical changes in bases would accumulate and eventually lead to mutations and disease.

Reasoning · why a whole glycosylase family exists

BER's specificity lives in its glycosylases — a family of enzymes, each tuned to one class of damaged base (uracil, oxidised guanine, alkylated bases, and so on). Why not one general enzyme? Because the damaged bases differ chemically, and mistaking a normal base for a damaged one would itself create a mutation. Dedicated recognisers keep the process both sensitive and safe — the same "get the target exactly right" theme as MMR's strand discrimination.

Clinical / real-world · why C→U repair matters so much

Spontaneous deamination of cytosine to uracil happens thousands of times a day in every cell — and it is exactly the C→U lesion Plate 4.3 repairs. This is why uracil is banned from DNA in the first place: if uracil were a normal DNA base, the cell couldn't tell a deamination accident from a legitimate letter. Defects in BER glycosylases (e.g. MUTYH) cause an inherited polyposis and colorectal cancer, echoing the repair-deficiency → cancer pattern.

§4.5Nucleotide excision repair (NER)

Where BER fixes a single wrong base, NER handles bulky damage that bends or distorts the DNA double helix — DNA lesions from ultraviolet light (thymine/pyrimidine dimers) and large chemical adducts from environmental mutagens. Specialised proteins patrol the DNA and recognise when the helix is distorted; on detecting a lesion they recruit others that cut the strand on both sides of the damage, removing a short single-stranded stretch. Plate 4.4 makes the "cut on both sides" logic clear.

Label Key — Plate 4.4
Pyrimidine (thymine) dimer
The bulky UV lesion — two adjacent pyrimidines bonded together, kinking the helix. This distortion is what the patrol proteins detect.
Excision nuclease
Cuts the damaged strand on both sides of the lesion (the two arrowheads) — the defining move that isolates the whole distorted stretch.
DNA helicase
Unwinds and removes the cut piece, leaving a ~12-nucleotide gap — much larger than BER's single-base gap.
DNA polymerase + ligase
Fill the 12-nt gap from the intact strand and seal it, restoring the helix.

So NER is the cell's main defence against bulky, helix-distorting damage — protecting against UV light and chemical mutagens.

Reasoning · why NER removes a whole patch, not one base

BER's glycosylases recognise a specific chemical lesion; NER instead recognises a physical one — the distortion a bulky adduct or dimer forces on the helix. It cannot know the exact identity or extent of the damage, so it plays safe and excises a generous ~12-nucleotide block around the kink, guaranteeing the lesion is gone. Different problem (shape vs single-base chemistry) → different solution (patch vs point) → different gap size. That contrast is the cleanest way to keep BER and NER apart.

Clinical / real-world · xeroderma pigmentosum

If NER is defective the consequences are severe. Xeroderma pigmentosum is a rare autosomal recessive disorder in which patients are extremely sensitive to sunlight and have a greatly increased risk of skin cancer; mutations in at least eight different NER genes have been linked to it. Because they cannot remove UV dimers, everyday sunlight causes mutations to pile up in skin — the starkest possible demonstration that a repair defect is a cancer risk.

§4.6Repair of double-strand breaks

The most dangerous lesion of all is a double-strand break (DSB) — both strands severed at once — caused by ionising radiation or drugs, or arising spontaneously after replication. DSBs are especially hazardous because they carry the risk of losing chromosomal material or causing chromosomal translocations (linking §4 straight back to §3.2). Two major pathways repair them, and which one runs depends on the cell-cycle phase: non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) predominates in G1 and early S phase, whereas homologous recombination (HR) becomes more important in late S and G2.

NHEJ repairs a break with no requirement for homology — it rapidly sticks the broken ends back together before the fragments drift apart. As Plate 4.5 shows, Ku heterodimers recognise the ends, specialised nucleases "clean" them, and ligases rejoin them. It is not very accurate: nucleotides are always lost during the cleaning process. Usually that loss is harmless — unless the lost bases fall in a gene coding region or a regulatory region. NHEJ can also introduce chromosomal translocations if unrelated DNA ends are joined together.

Label Key — Plate 4.5
Double-strand break
Both strands cut — no intact template remains at the break, which is why this pathway can't restore the exact sequence.
Ku heterodimers
Recognise and bind the broken ends, holding them together so they don't drift apart before rejoining.
Processing of DNA ends
Nucleases "clean" the ragged ends before ligation — the step that always loses nucleotides.
Ligation → deletion
The ends are rejoined, but the repaired DNA has "generally suffered a deletion of nucleotides." Harmless unless it hits a coding/regulatory region.

Homologous recombination is the accurate alternative: it uses the undamaged sister chromatid as a template. To initiate repair a nuclease digests the 5′ ends of the two broken strands; the exposed 3′ end of one broken strand then "invades" the intact homologous sister chromatid, searching for the complementary sequence to use as a template and elongating past the break point. The newly repaired strand is then used as the template to synthesise the other broken strand. Because it relies on the sister chromatid, HR occurs shortly after DNA replication but before cell division, when the sister chromatids lie close together. Plate 4.6 walks the full sequence.

Label Key — Plate 4.6
Nuclease digests 5′ ends
Resects the broken ends to expose single-stranded 3′ overhangs — the searching tips.
Strand exchange / invasion
A 3′ end pairs (by complementary base-pairing) with the intact sister chromatid, using it as a correct template.
Repair polymerase synthesis
Extends the invading strand along the undamaged DNA, copying the lost sequence back accurately.
Resolution & ligation
The invading strand is released, the second broken strand is copied, and ligation restores both duplexes — the double-strand break is accurately repaired with no lost information.
Reasoning · why the cell cycle decides NHEJ vs HR

HR's accuracy depends on having an identical template nearby — the sister chromatid. That only exists after replication (late S / G2), when the chromosome has been copied and the two sisters lie side by side. In G1/early S there is no sister to copy from, so the cell falls back on NHEJ, accepting a small deletion as the price of joining the ends quickly. So the choice isn't about preference — it is about whether an accurate template is physically available. Cause (cell-cycle stage) → mechanism (template present or not) → consequence (accurate vs error-prone repair).

Clinical / real-world · BRCA and homologous recombination

The BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes are essential for homologous recombination repair of double-strand breaks. Inherit a faulty copy and cells must rely on error-prone NHEJ, so breaks are mended with deletions and translocations — mutations accumulate, driving hereditary breast and ovarian cancer. It also cuts the other way therapeutically: because BRCA-mutant tumour cells already can't do HR, blocking their backup base-repair (PARP inhibitors) kills them selectively — a repair defect turned into a treatment.

The four repair pathways at a glance
PathwayDamage it fixesSignature enzymes / logicAccuracy
Mismatch (MMR)Wrong base missed by proofreadingMutS/MutL bind & scan to a nick on the new strandAccurate (strand-specific)
Base excision (BER)Single damaged base (oxidation, deamination, alkylation)Glycosylase → AP endonuclease → pol + ligaseAccurate
Nucleotide excision (NER)Bulky, helix-distorting lesions (UV dimers, adducts)Excision nuclease both sides → helicase removes ~12 ntAccurate
DSB — NHEJDouble-strand break (G1/early S)Ku ends → clean → ligateError-prone (loses nucleotides)
DSB — HRDouble-strand break (late S/G2)Resect 5′ → invade sister chromatid → copyAccurate (templated)
Memory hook · match the pathway to the lesion

"One base? BER. Big and bent? NER. Copy slip? MMR. Both strands snapped? Join it (NHEJ) or copy the sister (HR)."

Repair-deficiency cancers, one per pathway: MMR → Lynch/HNPCC, NER → xeroderma pigmentosum, HR → BRCA breast/ovarian.

R Recall checklist — DNA damage & repair
  • Damage becomes a mutation — only if it is left unrepaired and then copied by replication.
  • Three shared steps — excise, fill (polymerase, from the intact strand), and seal (ligase).
  • Mismatch repair — is strand-specific, using nicks in the new strand; its loss causes Lynch syndrome (HNPCC).
  • Base excision repair — a glycosylase removes a single damaged base (leaving an abasic site).
  • Nucleotide excision repair — cuts both sides of a bulky lesion and removes ~12 nt; its loss causes xeroderma pigmentosum.
  • NHEJ — joins broken ends with no homology, always loses nucleotides, and can cause translocations.
  • Homologous recombination — accurate repair using the sister chromatid as a template in late S/G2; needs BRCA.
